# 009 · A codec that loads whatever class a Kafka message names

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✗ Violation: 1 capability change** | security | critical | feature, behaviour change not intended | [`MessageCodec#decode`](../../examples/apps/boxoffice/contracts/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/boxoffice/contracts/MessageCodec.java) | [B10: Capability contracts](../../examples/tools/contracts/README.md) |

> To let one consumer decode messages of either family, the codec writes the Java class name into every payload and resolves it with Class.forName when reading. Round-trip tests pass. The module's capability contract now lists reflection, with the call site: the shape of the Jackson and XStream deserialization CVEs, caught without a CVE database.

## The change

An audit consumer wants to read both Kafka topics with one decoder, without a switch over message families that has to be extended for every new message. So `encode` adds a `class` field with the record's class name, and a new `decode(String)` reads it back with `Class.forName` and asks Jackson to build that class. Small, general, and it removes a chore. The developer does not mean to change what the module can do, only how it is used.

**Before** ([`MessageCodec.java`](../../examples/apps/boxoffice/contracts/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/boxoffice/contracts/MessageCodec.java), line 1):

```java
package net.terminalvalue.boxoffice.contracts;

import tools.jackson.databind.DeserializationFeature;
import tools.jackson.databind.json.JsonMapper;

/**
 * The JSON wire format of every message. Both services use this class, so they agree on the format whatever their
 * own Jackson settings are. The type is in the payload ({@code "type": "ChargePayment"}), not in a header that names
 * a Java class, so producers and consumers can be deployed independently.
 */
public final class MessageCodec {

    // ...
    private MessageCodec() {}

    public static String encode(Message message) {
        return MAPPER.writeValueAsString(message);
    }

    /** Throws {@link tools.jackson.core.JacksonException} for a payload that is not a {@code type}. */
```

**After:**

```java
package net.terminalvalue.boxoffice.contracts;

import tools.jackson.databind.DeserializationFeature;
import tools.jackson.databind.JsonNode;
import tools.jackson.databind.json.JsonMapper;
import tools.jackson.databind.node.ObjectNode;

/**
 * The JSON wire format of every message. Both services use this class, so they agree on the format whatever their
 * own Jackson settings are. The type is in the payload ({@code "type": "ChargePayment"}), and so is the Java class
 * ({@code "class"}), so that a consumer can decode any message without knowing its family up front.
 */
public final class MessageCodec {

    // ...
    private MessageCodec() {}

    public static String encode(Message message) {
        ObjectNode node = MAPPER.valueToTree(message);
        node.put("class", message.getClass().getName());
        return MAPPER.writeValueAsString(node);
    }

    /** Decodes a message of any family: the payload's {@code class} field names the record to build. */
    public static Message decode(String json) {
        JsonNode tree = MAPPER.readTree(json);
        String className = tree.path("class").asString();
        try {
            return (Message) MAPPER.treeToValue(tree, Class.forName(className));
        } catch (ClassNotFoundException e) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown message class " + className, e);
        }
    }

    /** Throws {@link tools.jackson.core.JacksonException} for a payload that is not a {@code type}. */
```

## What the verifier found

The module's bytecode now reaches 1 capability differently from its contract:

| Capability | The contract lists | The bytecode now has |
|---|---|---|
| `reflection` | *(nothing)* | `net.terminalvalue.boxoffice.contracts.MessageCodec.decode calls java.lang.Class.forName` |

Every call from the module's compiled code to a JDK entry point of a capability is listed, with the method that makes it, so the finding points at the exact call site.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

No: every existing unit test passes (`:contracts:test`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

Anyone who can write to the topic, or to anything that ends up on it, now chooses which class the ticketing and payment services instantiate from attacker-controlled fields. That is the exact mechanism of CVE-2017-7525 and its successors in Jackson, and of the XStream and Java deserialization gadget chains: a class name in the data, a framework that obligingly constructs it, and somewhere on the classpath a class whose constructor or setter does something dangerous. Dependency scanners find nothing, because no dependency is vulnerable; the application wrote the vulnerability itself. The original design comment, which said the type is a name in the payload and not a Java class for exactly this reason, was edited away in the same change.

## Why the verdict is right

The capability contract of the `contracts` module is computed from its compiled classes: every call to a JDK entry point that reaches beyond pure computation, grouped by capability, and every library it calls. Before the change the module uses no capability at all. After it, the verifier finds `Class.forName` in `MessageCodec.decode`, lists it under `reflection`, and fails the build because the checked-in contract does not grant it. The argument is one of absence turned into presence: a module whose bytecode never names a reflective entry point cannot load a class by name, and this one now does, at a line the finding points to.

## What to do

Keep the family in the API: decode with the sealed interface, which already carries the allowed subtypes as an explicit list, and route the audit consumer through a small switch on the two families. If a generic decoder is really wanted, map the `type` name through an allowlist the codec owns, never through the class loader, and the contract stays reflection-free.
